utterances.text: Administration for border police, foreign nationals, and administrative affairs headed by me, I was the deputy chief of the administration; number 6, the fire prevention police administration, headed by General Spasic, I don't remember his first name; analysis administration, Colonel Slobodan Krstic, if I'm not mistaken; administration for information and technology, Colonel Dragan Anucovic -- Anucojic, Anucojic with a J; communications administration headed I think by Joksic, I'm not sure if I got the name right, Joksic or Joksovic, and I definitely can't remember his first name; administration for joint affairs of the ministry headed by Gojko Todorovic; and administration for food supplies and accommodation headed by Popovic, I can't remember his first name. Most of these were colonels by rank. Whenever I'm not saying general, that means I'm talking about a colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Can we please now have Article 6 in both versions of the document. I think the page number was 8. You see Article 6, sir, don't you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Based on Article 6 of the rules says which other organizational units were set up in the public security sector?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: It reads here that in addition to the organizational units established by these rules in order to dispatch business under Article 2, and those are the organizational units that we've been talking about, special and separate police units are now being set up, OGs, operations groups, or rather, special units. That's what the article says.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the time we are discussing, which organizational units were eventually set up pursuant to Article 6, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm positive about two of those, there was the special anti-terrorist unit, we used to call it the SAI, and the helicopter unit was the other. I can't remember if there were any others in addition to these two, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The order in which these administrations are listed in Article 13, what does that suggest to you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: The order for the most part seems to be following an order that was perhaps established under a law, some law. Obviously those mentioned first are those more important or more serious, such as serious crimes. After that you normally have to deal with public law and order, traffic safety, and such concerns. That was the standard for the order in which these organizational units are mentioned. This was some sort of a ranking, if you like, some sort of hierarchy. Not each of these organizational units ranked the same in terms of salary for their employees in terms of ranks. You see that some of these heads are colonels, they couldn't go any higher than that, and some held a higher rank because their administrations dealt with more serious matters and they were in charge of managing a greater number of employees. Therefore, the order seems to be that of the degree of seriousness or difficulty entailed in their respective areas of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You've answered this, but was there any difference in terms of their salaries?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We shall now be leaving this subject matter concerning status and structure. For as long as you were at the seat of the ministry, did you ever hear or know of any plan to expel Albanians from Kosovo and Metohija in 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: No. It's not that I didn't know. I don't think a plan like that ever existed. I simply can't believe that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about you, were you ordered by anyone at any point in time to seize personal identification documents from Albanians crossing the Albanian -- the Kosovo and Metohija-Albanian border and Macedonian border and to destroy those documents?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you ever issue any such instructions to the SUPs or did you ever perhaps order any of the border police stations to take that course of action?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in the summer of 1998 Vlastimir Djordjevic and Obrad Stevanovic between late July and October ever spent any time in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't specify the time-period. I know that they did not attend collegium meetings on a regular basis, but I know that they spent some time in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know that Obrad Stevanovic was in Kosovo and Metohija throughout for the duration of the air-strikes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, Mr. Lukic, that's very much a leading question, isn't it? What you should be asking is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If he knows where he was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- what he knows rather than tell him a specific version that perhaps you wish to hear -- I don't know, but it sounds very leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's move on, sir. I am now returning to your own administration. The administration in which you were working was called administration of the border police for foreign nationals and administrative affairs. In order to hurry things along can we just refer to it from now on as border police administration?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't oppose that, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So what about this border police administration, did it have any organizational units on the ground that were part of its set-up?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it had border police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who appointed commanders to these border police stations?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Chief of sector following proposals by the head of the border police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who had the power to remove them or replace them?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Same as before, the chief of sector and the procedure followed was much the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know what Sreten Lukic's job was before he was dispatched to Kosovo and Metohija in June 1998?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was working as assistant chief of the Belgrade SUP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My understanding of the chief of sector would be Djordjevic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of the public security sector. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, to be clear. It seems odd that every police station commander should be appointed by him, but that's what it comes to, that Djordjevic hired and fired. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is correct. However, it was always following a proposal by the chief of sector who had the main say in it. The chief of sector would only decide on it, or rather, issue a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In the document we have, which is 6D1305 and P1072, in 6D1305, at page 14, we can see paragraph 2 and in P1072 at page 20, paragraph 2, please, Article 18. Page 16, 6D1305. In paragraph 2 or in Article 2 can we see the organization of the border police administration at headquarters, that is, its departments and stations of border police?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please explain the organization of the border police administration.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: According to Article 18 and its second paragraph, it reads that the administration comprises three departments, the department for border affairs; the department for foreigners and travel documents, being a separate department; and the department for administration affairs. It is further elaborated in stating that the department for border affairs, which is part of the administration, had its branch offices, one of which is called the branch office for border police and special conditions of international traffic -- excuse me, no. After that we have border police stations. I interpreted it wrongly. They are not part of the department, but they are answerable directly to the department for border police which is part of the administration. These stations are organizational units the same as the offices between -- within the border police department.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is this an exception compared to the other administrations at the seat of the ministry?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: The exception could be that the other administrations do not have territorial organizational units. They only have organizational units at the headquarters, and the entire issue of working in the field apart from the control of crossing the border falls within the competence of the organizational units of the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This administration through its border police stations, what is its immediate task in the field, direct task?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: The administration through its stations performs part of the work concerning border issues, including those which pertain to the control of border crossings at the physical border crossings, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know which border police stations were in Kosovo and Metohija in 1998 and 1999 and at which border crossings?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I am familiar with that. There was the border police station called Djeneral Jankovic, it covered two border crosses, the road crossing at Djeneral Jankovic and the railroad crossing at Djeneral Jankovic or Kacanik. The other station of border police was called Globocica, it covered only one border crossing, that of Globocica. All three border crossings were between the FRY and Macedonia. Then there were those to Albania. There were two stations, one was Vrbnica, with the same border crossing, and Cafa Prusit and the name of the border crossing was the same, so those police stations included only one border crossing each. The next station was at the airport in Pristina, which dealt only with the airport border crossing. There were five stations in total.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I don't know whether this is important or not, but I do not understand who the border police stations are answerable to in the administration in Belgrade. You told us -- the witness told us there are three departments, but none of them has a name that appears to encompass the border police stations. So who is it they answer to? Is it directly to some individual or is it to one of the sections within the border police administration in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will try to clarify this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dujkovic, you heard His Honour's question. Can you answer the question?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Your Honour, these border police stations were parts of the department for border affairs being one of the three departments within the administration. They -- the commanders of those stations were answerable to the chief of the department --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You have now answered it, but in our English transcript that was not originally presented but that clarifies it. Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Another clarification, please. You said that there was a border police station at the airport in Pristina. For example, were there any differences between the airports in Pristina and Nis?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, there was no difference. There, there was another border police station as well which was in charge of that particular border crossing and it was part of the administration department as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is outside the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, but however it is close to Pristina?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who provided the equipment for the border police stations to be able to operate?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: It was provided by the Ministry of the Interior. Most frequently it was following a request of the administration, a request sent from the field, and it was done through the logistics administration joint affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who determined what the principal tasks of border police stations were when it comes to their work pertaining to the border -- state border?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: The administration of border police --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his answer. The interpreter missed a part of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, part of that answer has been missed, if you could clarify it for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is not in the transcript. Could you please respond again to the question: Who determined the principal tasks of border police stations concerning their work at the state border?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Those tasks were determined by the Ministry of the Interior, and within the ministry the bulk of responsibility lay with the border police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did border police stations create their own work-plans?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, each and every station of border police had their own work-plan, which had to contain the principal tasks and activities determined by the ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the process of approving the work-plans of border police stations, could you please explain. Was each work-plan approved or were instructions given?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: No work-plan was approved separately. Each commander would have to draft a plan and forward it to the border police administration at the seat of the ministry. The administration, or rather, those responsible, if they had any suggestions to make they could forward them to the station commander so that he could amend his plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the foreigners' administration, did they have their own plans?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the administration of border police?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the administration has its own work-plan, which is also drafted based on the principal tasks received by the ministry and the minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who approves the work-plans of the border police administration?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: The chief of sector, the same way as before.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who provides instruction on the activities or work of border police stations?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Such direct instructions were given by the administration of the border police and the chief of the aforementioned department of border police, which is a part of the administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The instructions or requests for the work of border police stations, can they be made by other administrations as well?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Other administrations cannot provide instructions, but they can make certain operational requests; and in that case, stations could follow their requests. If they needed to issue instructions for the border police stations, it was done in agreement with the administration itself and it would be done through the administration and forwarded to the respective police stations.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can the minister issue instructions in your line of work?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, the minister can.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What kind of reports are submitted by border police stations?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Border police stations submit reports which can differ pertaining to the issue at hand or the event at hand. They can be urgent and periodical, once a month or once a year, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who are those reports submitted to?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: To the administration of border police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is the MUP staff in Kosovo and Metohija or anyone from the staff, could they instruct or order anything to the border police stations?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: It wouldn't be advisable without the knowledge of the border police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the level of the ministry, what sort of communication is there from the level of the border police stations?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean between the border police stations and the ministry?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: There are different types of or means of communication, via telephone, via dispatches sent to the ministry, and through written reports sent by couriers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the air-strikes began, were you able to use all these means of communication?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: After the bombardment, communication was made very difficult depending on NATO forces' activities, and there were frequent interruptions. Such interruptions were mainly restrictive. Individual means of communication were inoperative. We used telephone lines or we would lend telephone lines from other entities such as our organizations or individual citizens; however, it was difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you recall whether you could establish a telephone link say with border crossings or was it done through other organizational units?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: For the most part we communicated with the border crossings directly. The situation was not the same since there were many border crossings in Serbia as well as many police stations. With some communication was far easier, with some it was difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the border crossings in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Concerning those, as far as I know one could talk to them on the phone; however, those lines were down later for the most part. We were able to receive brief pieces of information with as little text as possible so as not to impose a burden on the system that was in place. However, I'm not very familiar with the technical aspects of that. We would draft a message and we would hand it over to the competent communications service which had to come up with a way to transit that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you were doing -- when they were doing their job on the state border, what legislation was applied by border police stations?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Practically all the legislation that concerns the Ministry of the Interior, but mainly in their line of work, mainly laws regarding the crossing of state border and movement across border crossings, the legislation concerning foreign nationals and travel documents. There were three federal laws. One was the Law on State Border Crossing and Movement in the Border Belt; the second was the Law on the Movement of Residents and Foreign Nationals; and the third was the Law on Travel Documents of the Nationals of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, or in earlier times SFRY. Those were laws that were passed at the time of the previous Yugoslavia, but they are still in force today, they are still followed. And in addition to those laws they, as the organizational unit of the ministry and as policemen, they also applied all other legislation relevant to the Ministry of the Interior, mainly republican legislation, such as the laws on the safety of traffic, laws on public order and peace, criminal legislation, et cetera. Although they are called border police, they were in fact universal organizational units because they had to act according to procedure whenever an incident or a criminal act occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, during the air-strikes were documents checked at border crossings in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: They were regularly checked up to a certain moment when there occurred a flooding of the state border by people wishing to cross, most of whom had no documents at all. This was directly linked to the situation on the ground, it had to do with the deterioration caused by the war and those people, judging by their appearance, their conduct, and everything else, looked like people who were in danger. They were looking for safety elsewhere, and that caused a big push towards border crossings with Macedonia and Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know the usual number of policemen in one shift at one border crossing, and I mean border crossings in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the particular nature of Kosovo and Metohija, there could be four to seven policemen in one shift at a border crossing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what is the job of the policemen manning a border police station at a state border crossing?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: To control traffic across the border, to check the documents of all people crossing the border, to check the export and import of certain objects prescribed by the ministry, such as weapons, ammunition, printed matter. But they always did that in conjunction with the customs office because the customs office had its own competencies over these goods. And another one of their tasks was to prevent the import of prohibited materials, such as weapons, ammunition, drugs, narcotic drugs, that is, and other goods that are prohibited and that -- which are crime-related. And they also had the task to check the movement and stop certain people at the border crossing, and of course that goes without saying to protect themselves and all the personnel manning the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I did not announce and we'll not be using, but just for reference 3D1122 is the Law on the State Border Crossing and Movement Within the Border Belt. Now, based on that law I will ask you a couple of questions, although you don't have it in your set of documents --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, that document has not been admitted as yet, but if it's a law it should be done by agreement I would have thought. Mr. Visnjic may have the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do have the answer. I just received a report that the translation has been completed and it will soon be uploaded into e-court later today. Then we will make the submission we have to make regarding that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Dujkovic, what is the basic document for crossing the state border?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: A travel document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: How about an ID, can it be used to cross the state border?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Only if we have such an agreement with a neighbouring state.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1999 was there an agreement between the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on one hand and Macedonia or Albania on the other hand allowing people to cross the border just with an ID?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is the visa system?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: That is a system under which approvals are issued for a person to enter a state with a valid travel document or to leave a country. It's usually a clause that is entered into a travel document, and exceptionally it can also be issued on a separate piece of paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have been told that we may not use the document 3D1122, but just as a reference for my next question I will invoke Article 67 and ask you: Are any records kept at border crossings?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, records are kept, all the relevant records covering what the police do and what is going on at the border crossing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you enumerate some of the records that are kept at border crossings by the police.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I can. For instance, at every border crossing record is kept of the number of persons crossing the border, either going in or out of the country, especially, or rather, separately for foreign nationals and separately for local citizens. Records are kept of visas issued at border crossings or tourist cards. Records are kept of measures taken towards persons crossing the state border, any case where the police exercised their powers is recorded. And one important record is the bulletin of daily events, wherein all incidents are entered chronologically with a description of the incident and the description of steps taken in response to that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now ask you something about representatives of the KVM. What was the approach to KVM representatives?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: That is the Kosovo Verification Mission. They were foreign representatives of the OSCE who stayed in Yugoslavia based on an agreement between Yugoslavia and the OSCE. Based on that agreement, they enjoyed diplomatic status, and that implied a certain treatment of them by the state authorities. I have to stress that people on the ground were told specifically concerning the KVM to pay special attention, to be forthcoming, to accommodate them in every way, even above the usual standard.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How did representatives of the KVM prove their status?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: On the ground they would produce a diplomatic ID they received from our foreign ministry, and that document was issued based on their passport and their diplomatic visa with which they came into the country. But on the ground even that ID was sufficient.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Who has jurisdiction over issuing visas and IDs for representatives of diplomatic missions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: The foreign ministry.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was the job of the police?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean in state border crossings or inland?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Everywhere.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean by the police, the police could only check their documents and visas that were in the passports. Holders of such passports are outside the competence of the police, the police may not ask for any additional visas, approvals, or take any other steps. They can just check their documents and put a stamp in their passport when they cross the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what was the job of the customs office?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: The customs service is generally responsible for controlling the transport of goods across the border, and as far as I know they too had to abide by international regulations governing these persons. But I cannot tell you exactly what exactly their entitlements were in relation to the transport of goods. I couldn't tell you, for instance, which goods these persons could take in and out duty-free, although I know that they had some entitles like that. But the attitude of the customs officers towards them was the same as that of the policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that you were informed by border -- the stations. Were you ever informed of any cases of mistreatment of persons crossing the state border?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: There may have been individual complaints by citizens about the work of the police, complaints about inappropriate behaviour, but it's not something that was allowed, authorised. Measures were taken against such policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were any instructions issued to that effect?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that kind of instruction could never be issued, it would be illegal from the outset.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What instructions were issued at that time, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time instructions were to increase alertness, to increase checks of persons crossing the border, primarily to prevent arms smuggling and to prevent people with all sorts of intentions and motives from crossing the border. And as far as members of the KVM and other diplomatic missions are concerned, the instruction was to act professionally and treat them fairly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Speaking of civilians, when did people begin to leave Kosovo and Metohija, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: If you mean large migrations, in the 1990s certain categories of the population left in greater numbers than usual, most of them legally but also illegally, mainly to western countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In 1999 when did the first mass movements of the -- sorry, 1999, when did the first mass movements of the population begin?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I want to know when it began.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: The date?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was there any event that would help you put a date on it, before or after the air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Just a day or two after the air-strikes started I believe people started crossing the border in large numbers, and later on there was an escalation, bottlenecks occurred on the border, and general crisis you might say began.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe it's -- we have to stop now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I was going to say is it a convenient time to interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we'll have our break at this stage. Mr. Dujkovic, we have to have a break at this stage for half an hour. Could you meanwhile please leave the courtroom with the usher. And we shall resume at ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [The witness takes the stand].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we continue, sir?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We were talking about the civilians leaving before the break, weren't we? What about border police stations, did those keep any records about that and were they submitting any chronological or statistical report?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Concerning these persons crossing the state border, the border police stations kept certain statistical records showing the numbers of people crossing the state border, and this was done in terms of their ethnic breakdown or citizenship. There were two categories in practical terms: Nationals and foreigners. Nothing more specific than that in terms of these persons' origin. There were no individual lists if that's what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the air-strikes started and large numbers of people started leaving Kosovo and Metohija, was it still possible to maintain regular checks in terms of checking travel documents and anything else that that entailed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: When the border crossings started being clogged up, because the borders were flooded with people, even women and children, arriving at the border with no proper travel documents to their names, it was impossible to go on checking their documents. Some of them were not even in the possession of appropriate documents. This wasn't something that could be done over a short period of time because on account of the lie of the land along the border there were bottlenecks forming there. I apologise, I have to say this too. In the neighbouring territory the situation was not quite the same as on our side in terms of the regime that these checks entailed. On the other side, as far as I knew, checks were even more rigorous in terms of holding people back and it's possible that they even made lists containing the names of all the individuals crossing the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You say in the neighbouring territory, what exactly do you mean?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I mean the territory of the neighbouring state, the neighbouring country, and I mean the work performed by their border police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Which country do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Specifically when I talk about those border crossings in Kosovo, I mean Macedonia and Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with any specific examples of the state border being crossed elsewhere, not at any of the official border crossings or with no valid travel documents at roughly the same point in time but something that didn't have to do with Kosovo and Metohija necessarily?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know several examples of circumstances like that arising, even under the Law on State Borders that applied at the time it was possible to allow persons to cross the border in places with no designated border crossings. In the case of major emergencies, the natural disasters, or anything in particular that was outside the ordinary going on in the neighbouring territory, for example, war or armed clashes, any situation in which the lives of civilians might have been at risk. I'm familiar with several such examples in more recent history, for example, along the border to Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Likewise, a large number of people crossed into Serbia's territory without being checked. It wasn't possible to check those persons simply because those persons in the majority of cases carried no travel documents or maybe they were carrying travel documents or other documents that would not have entitled them to cross a state border. They weren't valid travel documents. Those were refugees or persons who had been expelled from their homes, mostly from Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and these people were trying to cross the border and enter Serbia. In this case also we were facing large numbers of people, sometimes tens of thousands, attempting to make the crossing, sometimes as many as 100.000 or more. And this happened more than once. I'm talking about attempted crossings from Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina. Some examples from a more remote past based on my own experience, I'm talking now about the border to Romania during the revolution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the relevance of this? At the moment I don't even know where the witness is saying that there were -- there was the possibility of crossing into Macedonia or Albania at points other than the official border crossings, but I do know a bit more about Croatia, Bosnia, and I am about to learn about Romania. Now, are these of relevance to us?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just trying to explain Balkans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. It's a matter for you to decide if you think that's going to help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We won't dwell for too long on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You started telling us about Romania, sir, briefly, if you can, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, similar circumstances prevailed at the time. People from Romania were crossing the state borders at official border crossings and elsewhere. Because of the upheaval in Romania at the time, the fall of Ceausescu. If I may complete this thought, there had been a situation like that in Hungary a long time ago back in 1956 with the Soviet invasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The Presiding Judge has just instructed us as to what he would like to hear. What about Albania and Macedonia, did people only take the official border crossings to get into Macedonia and Albania or did they also attempt to cross elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and on a massive scale. It wasn't even possible for them to use the official border crossings since this was an area that was teeming with their own armed units. Therefore, it would not have been advisable to use any other possibility. The only option was to use the official border crossing because that was the only safe option to pick. It is possible that crossings occurred elsewhere, but certainly not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know whether there was any order at any point in time issued by your administration or the foreign ministry to destroy personal identification documents?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, no such order could possibly have been issued and no such action taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say, I don't see how there would have been any purpose to anything like that, let me ask you this: Can you please explain what types of records were kept in relation to Serbia's and Yugoslavia's citizens?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean at border crossings?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: You mean the police or generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, what I know is this: Each citizen has several different records. When they're born, their information is entered into what we call the birth register, two separate copies of this document are kept, even in separate buildings, because that's what the regulations say must be done, that's the procedure. There are similar types of records as well kept in the same place as the birth register, I'm talking about the death register and the marriage register as well as what we called the book of citizens. But this is under a different ministry, this is not something that the Ministry of the Interior does. These are birth, marriage, and death register offices and they keep these records. Based on such records, a person can always get a special certificate issued based on the information contained therein. As for the Ministry of the Interior, likewise they keep records about status and about individual citizens. From the moment of birth as soon as a person is recorded into the birth register, the notary or birth register official must forward this type of information to the Ministry of the Interior; then the Ministry of the Interior, based on this, determines a personal identification number for each and every citizen because it's the ministry that must determine this number, assign this number, and keep track of it. This is then submitted, the other copy of the birth register, to the Ministry of the Interior. Each person from their birth on must be registered by the Ministry of the Interior, also in order to keep track of their place of residence. This is what we call the population register, and each person must be recorded in that document, in that book. Based on this, as soon as a person comes of age there are certain entitlements and rights that this person can now exercise. For example, having an ID issued and some other rights that have to do with a person's residence. In relation to this residence register, there is a type of record that is set up earlier on. IDs issued to all those who under the law are entitled to have one issued. There are several types of records, so many in fact, that it would have been impossible for a person to simply not be recorded anywhere at all. Information on this type of thing would certainly have been preserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: For example, the ID register, what exactly does it comprise?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: The ID register is kept in several different ways, one way being this. Each person applying for an ID is recorded in a register, in a book, this is a handwritten entry, those made containing all the information that is required. Next, based on any information contained in a written application by that person, a personal file is compiled and deposited in a ledger, in a system of files which is normally in alphabetical order. And then all of this is transformed into an electronic database. So to all practical intents there are three different ways to record this type of situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the citizen identification number. We haven't discussed this yet, but can you tell us if one looks at that number what exactly can one tell, how many digits?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: 13 digits. If you look at it you can tell the person's age, date of birth, and not everyone can tell but those who are familiar with the system can see all of this including a person's place of residence. There are some other numbers there which are mainly used to distinguish between various people in order to preclude the possibility of two persons ending up with the same number. This has to be computerised because that allows us to monitor the situation, and this applies throughout Serbia, just to keep accidents from happening, for example, someone being awarded the same number and issued in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is a separate register, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is a separate register that separate laws and special regulations apply to, and this is something that in our country is under the jurisdiction of the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At what age is this number assigned?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: At birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know if these records, registers, and files were relocated before the air-strikes started?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: That depended on the secretariat, but for the most part those records were put away somewhere safe. For example, some ledgers, some registers, were taken elsewhere and sometimes entire files were moved, these files were sometimes quite extensive and bulky. There were some cases in Belgrade in some major cities where they couldn't be moved because they were to hefty, rather, there was an attempt to protect them in a different way. Most of the ledgers and registers were put away somewhere safe and then many different measures were taken at the time in order to preserve these records.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about after the war, did anyone come into the possession of these records in Kosovo and Metohija; and if so, who?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Once the war was declared over and once the UNMIK administration had entered Kosovo based on my memory and on reports that I received, field reports, for the most part those records were officially handed over. Sometimes they were simply left behind sometimes on the account of the situation that prevailed on the ground at the time. And then the UNMIK people simply took possession of those records and registers of their own accord. As far as I know, most of the records have been preserved. I think in the Kosovska Mitrovica secretariat some of the RD files were destroyed, but the ledgers and registers have been preserved. Regardless of that, this is all part of the electronic database which I assume must be in a safe place, the server, that is, maybe it's even outside Kosovo. I'm not familiar with its exact whereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All of the records we mentioned, do they distinguish between citizens based on their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not a single one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I just ask one thing before we move away from it. You were there until or you worked until 2005; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I worked at the administration -- excuse me, no. At the administration of border police and foreigners I worked there until 2000. After that I was sent to another organizational unit of the ministry, this being the police school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And when you left to go to the police school, you would be aware then where the server was for the electronic database, I assume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this was not within our purview. We didn't need to know these technical details. I don't know about that. I might inquire informally and we might be able to find it out, otherwise there was no need for me to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You seem to know a lot of detail, but -- and you seem to know that there is an electronic database or is that something you're speculating about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I know for sure that there is an electronic database, but I don't want to speculate as to its technical aspects. I can only presume that due to technical reasons those servers may be in three different locations, maybe more. For sure one of them is in Belgrade where the seat of the ministry is. As for Vojvodina, which is another province of ours, I know that the servers can also be found in Novi Sad for technical reasons. They had already been there during a period of time, and then when there were some changes within governmental structures and relations between different bodies of the state, it simply remained there and was not physically transferred to Belgrade. I don't know whether it applies to Kosovo and Metohija as well, though. For some reasons, these may have stayed there or may have been connected to some other servers. I don't know such details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: To follow Judge Bonomy's line of questions, I wanted to ask you whether you could access those servers from your work station, from your office.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: From my office I could access all records that I had been authorised to use. Personally I didn't deal with that since I had no time or need to, but my clerks, my employees, within the administration following their job descriptions were able to use such registers. Very few requests or tasks can be resolved without establishing contact with that database first.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that, for example, even Slovenia can use that system?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Maybe at the time when the SFRY was still a single state, there may have been such links; but after that each of the republics established its own information system. As to any mutual cooperation between the systems relies on the people working there. I don't know whether there was such a possibility to enter any records of other republics.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What is your administration in charge of?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: The administration I used to work for had a broad range of competences. In a way, artificially it was turned into a single administration, whereas it should have been two or so. In any case, I know that two administrations were created subsequently within the ministry. As for border issues, that would be one. Another group would be the issues pertaining to the movements of foreigners and suppressing illegal migration. The third group of tasks would deal with travel documents of nationals. The fourth group of tasks would have to do with weapons and ammunition in possession of citizens and entities, and the last group of tasks would be the so-called legal affairs which dealt with things such as residence, personal identification numbers, issuing of IDs, public gatherings, and other administrative matters that we call them in our slang. However, some administrative issues are covered by other domains as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On top of all this, did you also work on the matters pertaining to legal residence of our citizens abroad?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of the tasks, the issue of issuing travel documents, suppressing and detecting abuse of travel documents, and the issues of our citizens residing abroad. Given that when they reside abroad they can also exercise certain rights pertaining to travel documents, and in that regard there should be a link established with our administration. It also deals with certain situations of our citizens residing abroad in case they need to return to the country, forcibly or against their wish. Then that would have to have been coordinated with our administration in other state organs. That was within the area pertaining to travel documents affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you something about identity cards in detail. For the sake of the transcript I will go over a few documents, but I will not be tendering them or using them here. We have the Law on the Issuing of IDs which is 6D1418, and the Law on Identity Cards which is P1832 [Realtime transcript read in error "P1382"]. In times of peace, Mr. Dujkovic, how old does one need to be to be issued with an ID?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: In normal peacetime situations under the law prescribing that, any person older than 18 has the right and obligation to be in possession of an ID.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could anyone get an ID if they were younger than 18; and if so, at what age?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, according to the rules such a situation was envisaged. A minor older than 15 could request to be issued with an ID, although there was no such obligation. People younger than 15 years of age under the law could be in possession of an ID if such a request was made by their custodians or parents; however, such situations occurred seldom. I don't even know of any of them. This is sort of a right they could enjoy, but I don't know what situations required that. Perhaps if someone needed to have a document which would assist in identifying a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: During my career I met such situations in cases when minors would complete marriages?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and if they were younger than 15 and if they wanted to exercise certain rights as minors and if they needed identification papers for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does the fact that minors do not possess IDs mean that they do not enjoy a certain status?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: That is incorrect. As I explained, when a person is born his or her parent or custodian and the institution where the birth took place, all these have to report the birth to the competent office and that person is entered into the birth register. What follows is the procedure I described. It all happens within a short period of time. The notary notifies the Ministry of the Interior, primarily in order to assign a personal identification number, and since we have another copy of the birth register and that needs to include the entry as well. The parent or the custodian is legally bound to have the newborn registered at a certain location so that the newborn could receive or have data about its residence. Otherwise such things are done following a request and only pursuant to the registers that exist with the relevant bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dujkovic, in your statement and also in other evidence we've heard we've been referred to a change made during the war reducing the age of which a personal identity card was compulsory to the age of 14. Do you know why that was the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are situations, for example, times of war when we have a state of war in place, then special regulation is put in place, decrees with the force of law, which bypass the regular legislative procedure and is put in place by other organs. For example, following a governmental proposal the president can sign such a decree. Such decrees are issued to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dujkovic, we know -- we've had evidence about that. All I want to know is whether you know why this change was made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. As far as I know, in the explanation that I could read it states that it was so that the work of the Ministry of the Interior in wartime conditions would be made easier. The explanation was rather brief and it is not under my direct competence; therefore, I had nothing to do with such initiatives. It is done by another office in our administration which deals with systematic legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You know no more than that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a regulation we had to implement and we did. I don't know what the reasons were behind it, at least no other reasons apart from the ones I stated to make the work of the ministry easier, since identifying persons in the field falls under the competence of the Ministry of the Interior. I personally think it was also in the best interest of those people so that they could enjoy their rights more easily. I noticed an interesting occurrence at the time, and that is that young men, mostly men, were proudly -- proud at the time to be able to possess an ID. We had queues and people came in in bundles asking for such documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So as far as you're aware, this had nothing to do with trying to get on top of the threat of young Albanian men taking up arms against Serbia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. That was not possible, since that regulation was uniform for the entire state. In practice it was used even more in other parts of the country than in Kosovo and Metohija. I'm trying to say that citizens were quite disciplined when respecting that regulation and it could not have been applied selectively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, could you then explain -- give me a concrete example of how this would make the work of the Ministry of the Interior easier in the time of conflict and how it would make people or give people the opportunity to enjoy their rights more easily in a time of conflict.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, for example, one of the ways for them to enjoy their rights in a more accessible way is to be less restricted in their movements. Since in such circumstances movement is hindered, sometimes even prohibited during certain periods. The competent bodies controlling the movement of persons in the field can establish their identity much more easily. The difference between a minor and an adult visually speaking is sometimes difficult to detect. On many occasions we have people who appear to be adults, but once you see his or her ID you realize it's a minor. This may have been one of the reasons why the age was reduced. It also has to do with another regulation on -- concerning the Law on Identity Cards, which states that people younger than 18 could also have IDs; however, this regulation made it obligatory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dujkovic, that would suggest to me that the objective was to exercise more control rather than to give more freedom, which would make sense of course. But lay that aside, it would appear from what you've said that the objective was to exercise more control over people between the age of 14 and 18.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I see that as a possibility for those people to be more secure. For example, a policeman might not be able to ascertain the identity of a person due to various circumstances, inability to establish communication, we don't know where his or her parents are, or movements of citizens, and it's in such circumstances easier to identify a person with an ID rather than going back to his parents to ascertain his or her identity since it may have been impossible in the given circumstances. It could be but one of the reasons and we could probably come up with more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, the two documents you referred to just a little while ago 6D1418 and P1382 are also not admitted at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 6D is not translated, so that's why I'm trying to avoid --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are these documents then to be the subject of a motion later?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sometimes the questions of us lawyers might appear to be meaningless but I still have to ask you: What if a person loses, damages, or destroys his or her own ID, for example, it ends up in a washing machine in the pocket of a shirt, is their status as a citizen thereby compromised?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: No, it's not. Obviously they can get this sort of document re-issued, even if it's lost. This is not something that needs proving. People are simply believed when they state that they have lost their ID. This is not something that is verified. Their identity is determined based on information already in our possession. Some files even contain photographs such as the ID register. If we're dealing with a person who is not in our records, no ID can be issued regardless of the person's statement or application.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, did the ID card itself have a photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What about the files, the print of the right index finger is to be found there too, right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What if a person loses, destroys, or damages their ID card somewhere abroad?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: This is seldom the case. This is not the type of situation that is frequently encountered because no person is under an obligation to carry ID on them abroad. As soon as they're back in their country of origin they'll apply for a new one. For example, if the situation is that our citizens can use their ID card to cross the border to another country, then this type of situation is reported to the relevant body in that other country. There are consular relations. This person is then allowed to return to their country of origin. As soon as they are back in their country of origin they can get a new document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What if a person loses, destroys, or damages their passport while abroad?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: If that is the case, they have to go to our embassy or consulate in that country in order to retrieve a new document allowing them to return to their country of origin or alternatively to stay in the country they find themselves in, for example, if they work in that country. These documents are issued following approval by the relevant bodies inside the country and this approval can only be issued once the relevant files have been inspected containing information about the applicant.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What if someone leaves the country with no personal documents on them, regardless whether these have been destroyed, discarded somewhere along the border or somewhere in the middle of Kosovo and Metohija, how would these persons be able to return with no documents while not being in possession of proper documents?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: These are standard situations and have nothing to do with the situations that we have been discussing today. What was happening along the border to Albania and Macedonia, but there were other situations. If we're dealing with a limited number of people, the procedure is the same, they have to report to the appropriate embassy or consulate, they had to shed light of the circumstances how this came about that they were now no longer in possession of their travel documents or any other documents, and their travel document is declared to be valid in order to facilitate their return to their country of origin. The procedure that is followed is the same. You can't have an application like that unless you have information from the files showing that this person is indeed a national and that they have residence in the Republic of Serbia. In such cases, applications of this nature simply cannot be turned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. And what sort of rule applies to those who left Kosovo and Metohija in 1999, is there some sort of legal decision about this and what do you think the procedure would have been that would have been followed in cases such as these?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think it's a legal solution for situations like these. All I can do is speculate at the time. Perhaps I can liken this to another situation that we have back in our country these days and for the last several years the same type of situation has prevailed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Dujkovic, can I just ask you to speak a little more slowly to assist the interpreters. Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. We have this situation and we still have it, tens of thousands, hundreds of thousands of our citizens, 150.000 citizens of ours happen to be somewhere abroad in Western countries, most of them in Germany, Switzerland, Austria, Norway, Sweden, and so on and so forth. How do these persons get there? Illegally or perhaps they had lost their legal status and then subsequently refused to return to our country. They are reluctant to return to our country. They apply to the appropriate bodies, mostly they state reasons such as their human rights being violated or in danger in our country. Many of these people end up as asylum seekers, that is what we call them. In the case of these people, their return might prove very difficult, firstly because they refuse this themselves, they will not do this of their own free will, and then secondly, those countries have the commitment to facilitate their return. And there is normally a separate procedure in place, there are agreements in place between our country and these other countries on particular cases and situations and the conditions under which these people can return to our country. And then the procedure takes its course. It's possible that there might be other similar agreements, and this is merely an assumption, between our country and those other countries where these persons happen to be who are illegally there. And this might facilitate their return. Maybe there might be another procedure in place that might turn out to be more or less complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you know if all the records have been preserved and passports and ID cards issued?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, all the records have been preserved. I'm not aware of a single case in which a person was refused the right to be issued with an ID or a document simply because their information was missing from the files. There have been cases of incomplete files or those that have not been preserved in their entirety. I talked about Kosovska Mitrovica, I know for sure about that one. I don't know about any other secretariat. I know that they kept the books, but the register was destroyed when the building, the MUP building, there was targeted by a shell or bombed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have 6D1324 brought up in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: This, just to make an observation, is another document that was notified to us after the time stipulated in the Court order, and also there is no translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, what do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's all true, Your Honour, but let me check one ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because only during the proofing with this witness we realized that we should -- this is the last chance to use this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, do you object to it being used? Is there a particular difficulty for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The difficulty of course is that when we are notified late about untranslated documents, there is very little we can do because of the resource limitations we have. However, if the witness is the only person, as I think is being represented by my friend, if the witness is the only person who can speak about the document, I don't know how we can responsibly maintain an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It seems a fairly short document. If you need any particular part translated, then it can be read. So we will allow you, Mr. Lukic, to use this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. And I thank my learned friend as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We have no translation for this document, Mr. Dujkovic. Can you please read who issued this document, when -- that's it for now.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: The header reads: "Office of the National Council for cooperation with the International Criminal Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia on the 11th of November -- on the 11th of September, 2007," signed by head of office Dusan Ignjatovic. This was submitted to counsel Dragan Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please read item 2.

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: Item 2 reads -- it literal says: "An individual named Sadiku Sadija born in 1978 in Kosovska Mitrovica residing in Zabare village, Kosovska Mitrovica municipality has no information on any personal documents issued this was checked through the records of Serbia's MUP, fine, and this has been established by checking the records of Serbia's MUP. It has been established that this person has not been registered or recorded."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After everything we've heard today, do you allow for the possibility that this person Sadiku Sadija --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... a very leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It sounds very leading, Mr. Lukic. I think you should simply ask him for his explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've heard the Presiding Judge. What's your explanation?

utterances.speaker: PETAR DUJKOVIC
utterances.text: My explanation is this person was not recorded anywhere, not in any of the registers discussed or mentioned today, specifically the body that ran its check looked for this information in Serbia's MUP and subsequently ascertained that this person's information was not to be found in any of the files including the electronic database, which means nowhere at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I do believe we have to break for the day, since our time seems to be up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I note that the area involved is Kosovska Mitrovica, where you said there had been a difficulty, but that would not explain the absence of records. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. What follows from this, in fact, is that this body has certain records based on which one might be able to ascertain beyond any doubt at all that this person was recorded, but this person was most certainly not recorded in the area of Kosovska Mitrovica or anywhere else in Serbia for that matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I -- I obviously didn't make myself clear. I thought that some records in Kosovska Mitrovica had been destroyed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. The ID files were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So that would not explain the total absence of records that -- in relation to this person; that's the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is right. What I'm trying to say is this person appears not to have been recorded in any of the various registers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I wonder if this could be conveniently dealt with here and now. I -- the transcript 85 -- page 85, 15 gives a name. I wonder if he could be asked to repeat the name. I don't think any name was recorded on the transcript in full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, 85, 15? Could you again, Mr. Dujkovic, look at item 2 in the document and give us again the name of the person.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. Sadija Sadiku, a lady.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Lastly, Your Honour, I think my friend erroneously referred to the law on identification cards as P1382 and indicated that that was not in evidence or had not been translated. It is in fact P1832, it is in evidence and has been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: End on a high, Mr. Lukic. Mr. Dujkovic, we have to bring our proceedings for the day to an end at this stage. Unfortunately we cannot finish your evidence today. You will have to come back tomorrow, that will be at 9.00 in this courtroom. Meanwhile between now and then it is an important rule that you have no communication whatsoever with anyone about any aspect of the evidence in this case. Because you're a witness in the witness box, there is no possibility of you discussing with anyone any aspect of the evidence. Please bear that in mind and return to resume your evidence at 9.00 tomorrow. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. For the attention of others, because of a Judges' plenary meeting tomorrow, our -- we'll be sitting rather unusual hours. The first session will be from 9.00 till 10.30; the next will be from 10.50 until 11.50, so just one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And then we will resume at 2.30 in the afternoon until 4.00, so until 9.00 tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
